title: Row-level security as enforcement
objective: Compile the read rule to row-level security policies, test them per user against the access matrix, find the owner bypass and fix it with FORCE, and exhibit an integrity-check channel as a pair of worlds.

blocks.md: Your policy has been facts and rules. Now the database has to enforce it, one row at a time.

choice.prompt: A row fails the `USING` clause of every policy that applies to a user's `SELECT`. What does the user get?

options.why: `USING` hides rows; it does not refuse the query.

options.text: Nothing: the row is silently left out.
options.why: The manual says such rows are "silently suppressed; no error is reported".
`WITH CHECK` governs new rows from `INSERT` and `UPDATE`.

choice.prompt: Every row a user can see passes the read policy. Can the user still learn that a row they cannot see exists?

options.why: A hidden row can still change an outcome.

options.text: Only if a policy is missing.
options.why: A complete policy still leaves those checks in place.

options.text: Yes: some checks run against every row, whoever may see it.
options.why: Uniqueness and foreign-key checks bypass row security.

blocks.md:
A worked example first. The lab template gives you the schema `documents(id, slug UNIQUE, team_id, title, body, internal_notes, shared_team_ids int[])`, with `memberships` and `shares`, and `user_teams(u)`, a function that returns a user's team closure from a recursive query, independent of the Datalog engine. For a user on no team it returns an empty array, never NULL. Your three rules become three policies.

Read them with three facts in mind. Permissive policies combine with OR, as your three rules did. When row security is on and no policy applies, a default-deny policy is used, so no row is visible. And a policy whose `USING` expression is NULL hides the row, as `WHERE` skipped NULL rows in S6, so an unset `app.user` fails closed.

blocks.direction: The cell loads the template world, creates your policies, and then runs frank's statement.

call.prompt: frank (Growth, viewer) holds the UPDATE privilege and runs `UPDATE documents SET title = 'x' WHERE id = 'q3-plan'`, a row invisible to him. What comes back?

options.why: `USING` filters before the update; it does not refuse the statement.
Such rows "will not be available for modification", and the manual's own example prints `UPDATE 0`.

options.text: The update succeeds, because UPDATE checks only `WITH CHECK`
options.why: `WITH CHECK` tests the new row, and `USING` tests the existing ones.

blocks.after: The row was filtered out before the update saw it, so nothing changed and nothing failed {{run:RUN-pg-rls-semantics}}. Now edit the cell: as dana, an editor, move q3-plan to Growth, where she is not an editor. That trips `WITH CHECK` and raises an error. `USING` filters rows that exist; `WITH CHECK` refuses rows that would be written.

choice.prompt: A variant of `read_team_shared` says `shared_team_ids <@ user_teams(...)` where yours says `&&`. On W0, for which (user, document) pair do the policies and the matrix disagree?

options.why: contract has no team shares, so its array is empty, and the empty array is contained in every array. frank now sees it.
Both versions allow it: roadmap's only team share is Payments, and dana is on Payments.
Rule 1 admits hal in both versions, so the two agree.

blocks.direction: The cell loads the template world with your policies unchanged, and then runs the application's query.

call.prompt: RLS is enabled and your policies are unchanged. The application connects as the owner of `documents` and sets `app.user` to frank. What does frank's query return?

options.why: The owner is not bound unless the table is forced.
Default deny applies to the roles row security binds, and the owner is not one yet.
The manual: "Table owners normally bypass row security as well, though a table owner can choose to be subject to row security with ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY".

blocks.after: Every document came back {{run:RUN-pg-rls-owner}}. Run it again after `ALTER TABLE documents FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;` as the owner, and frank's row returns. FORCE is configuration, so you read it back from `pg_class` with the time, and stamp it [C]. Three more facts about who row security binds. A policy limited `TO app_users` leaves the forced owner with nothing, since no policy applies to it. Superusers and roles with `BYPASSRLS` always bypass. And `app.user` is trusted only because no end user runs SQL, which the claim carries as an assumption [A].

choice.prompt: Which connection shows frank a document his policies deny him?

options.text: The table's owner, with RLS enabled and not forced.
options.why: Owners bypass row security unless the table is forced.

options.text: A member of `app_users`, with RLS enabled.
options.why: The policies bind members of `app_users`, forced or not.

options.text: The table's owner, with `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` on.
options.why: Forcing binds the owner to the same policies as everyone else.

segments.title: A channel the policy cannot see

blocks.md: Every read so far was filtered. Now look at a write. Slugs are globally unique in this schema, so a slug names a row for everyone, including rows a user cannot see.

blocks.direction: The cell loads the template world with your policies, and then runs frank's insert.

call.prompt: frank inserts a document with the slug 'layoffs-memo' into Growth. Birch already has a private document with that slug, invisible to frank. What happens?

options.text: The insert succeeds, because RLS hides Birch's row from the constraint
options.why: Constraint checks see every row.
The manual: "Referential integrity checks, such as unique or primary key constraints and foreign key references, always bypass row security to ensure that data integrity is maintained".
The refusal comes from the constraint, not from a policy.

blocks.after: The insert fails on the unique constraint {{run:RUN-pg-rls-covert}}, and the error carries no key: under row security the DETAIL line that would name the slug is withheld {{run:RUN-pglite-rls}}. In the paired world, where Birch has no such row, the insert succeeds. Two worlds differ only in Birch's private row, and frank tells them apart.

blocks.md:
Every read was filtered, and frank still learned a bit. The channel is the error class: a unique violation against a successful insert. It is one bit, not the slug's owner or value, and the manual tells schema designers to avoid exactly this "covert channel" through integrity checks (section 5.9). There are three cures: a constraint per tenant, `UNIQUE (tenant_id, slug)`; opaque identifiers; or a recorded release, which S7.L7 teaches. S7.L5 names what you just found: enforcing the read rule is not the same as noninterference.

One more channel, seen only on the Bench. A policy that reads another table can race with a change to that table. In the recorded run, a locking read returns the new text at READ COMMITTED and fails with a serialization error at the two stricter levels, so the race is prevented by failure, not by returning nothing {{run:RUN-pg-catalog}}.

choice.prompt: frank inserts a document with the slug 'budget' into Growth. Which pair of worlds, differing only in Birch's private rows, lets him tell them apart by the outcome?

options.text: Birch has a private document with the slug 'budget' in one world and none in the other.
options.why: One insert fails on the unique constraint and the other succeeds.

options.text: Birch's private document layoffs-memo has a different body in each world.
options.why: No constraint the insert touches reads a body, so the outcomes match.

options.text: Birch has a private document with the slug 'budget-2' in one world and none in the other.
options.why: A different slug collides with nothing, so the outcomes match.

choice.prompt: A table has row security enabled and forced, with one policy limited `TO app_users`. Its owner, who is not a member of `app_users`, connects and lists the rows. What does the owner see?

options.why: Forcing binds the owner, so the bypass is gone.
The policy applies to `app_users`, and the owner is not one.
Forced, the owner is bound, and no policy applies to it, so default deny leaves nothing.

choice.prompt: Which of frank's commands reveals whether Birch has a private document with the slug 'layoffs-memo'?

options.why: Row security filters before the count, so it is zero in both worlds.
It fails on the unique constraint when Birch has the row, and succeeds when it does not.
A hidden row is not available for modification, so it affects no row either way.

blocks.title: Twin
blocks.md: Cedar's third layer is daily differential random testing of its Rust authorizer against its Lean model. The paper [How We Built Cedar](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01688) reports that proofs found 4 bugs and differential and property-based testing found 21. Its generator finding, in section 4.3 of the [language paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04651), is why the lab's receipt prints generator statistics. Pins: {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}.

ROW H01 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: both commit, final 20, the second debit's write returns 20 -> 20. SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, is recorded: 40001.
ROW H02 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the waiting statement updates 0 rows. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, only expected before, are recorded: 40001.
ROW H03 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the DELETE removes 0 rows and a hits = 10 row exists before and after. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H04 [agrees]: The reader's two reads total 250 at READ COMMITTED and 200 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H05 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ with a team total of -100; at SERIALIZABLE the second committer fails with 40001 and the total is 50.
ROW H06 [agrees]: Both commit at READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ (160 held against 100); at SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001 and 80 stays held.
ROW H07 [agrees]: Run from the upstream specs: REPEATABLE READ gives s3 a state no serial order shows; SERIALIZABLE aborts s2 with 40001 (-2); DEFERRABLE makes s3 wait (-3).
ROW H08 [agrees]: 6 of 210 permutations fail with s3 READ ONLY; the READ WRITE variant is measured here, not read from the spec comment.
ROW H09 [agrees]: The second count is 3 at READ COMMITTED, 2 at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.
ROW H10 [agrees]: With one session SERIALIZABLE and the other READ COMMITTED both commit, in both assignments and both commit orders; with both SERIALIZABLE one fails with 40001.
ROW H11 [agrees]: A sequential scan aborts a SERIALIZABLE transaction that shares no row with the other; the same transactions on an index scan over distant keys both commit.

ROW H12 [agrees, with additions]: 23505 and 23P01 appear under SERIALIZABLE; which of 40001 and 23505 appears depends on whether the failing session checked first and on the order, and a whole-command retry with a re-check ends without error where a blind retry fails again.
ROW H13 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: the statement waits, then updates the row it could not see. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H14 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: 23505, no restart. REPEATABLE READ: 23505. SERIALIZABLE: 40001.
ROW H15 [agrees]: Disjoint claims at all three levels; the count through SKIP LOCKED is 0 while 4 jobs are pending.
ROW H16 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED returns the rows out of order; REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE raise 40001; FOR UPDATE in a subquery returns them in order.
ROW H17 [agrees]: READ COMMITTED: mallory sees 'secret from mallory'. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: her locking read fails with 40001, so it is prevented by failure.
ROW H18 [agrees]: CHECK accepts NULL, the guarded UPDATE skips the NULL row, USING hides it, WITH CHECK raises 42501; the same at all three levels.
ROW H19 [agrees]: 22003 'bigint out of range' at all three levels; the balance is unchanged; sum(bigint) is numeric.
ROW H20 [agrees]: Row 1 is never delivered: the mark is 2, both ids exist, the next poll returns nothing; the same at all three levels.
ROW H21 [agrees]: Both permutations of the regression test end with bar's 40001, the output the upstream file expects.

ROW H22 [differs]: Ascending order removes the deadlock and both commit at READ COMMITTED. At REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE, 4 of the 6 ascending-order permutations still fail with 40001 (first updater wins), so ordering is no substitute for the retry.
ROW H23 [agrees]: B's COMMIT fails with 40001; its retry reads 20 available, the guard refuses (0 rows) and nothing is written.
ROW H24 [agrees]: REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE: B fails with 40001 and its retry updates 0 rows. READ COMMITTED: no error, 0 rows.
notes: The tester is PostgreSQL's own isolationtester, built from the 18.6 source tarball and run against the Debian-packaged 18.6 server of the postgres:18 image; it is not statespace isorun (W4-T16).

isolationtester prints errors as 'ERROR:  <message>' without a SQLSTATE. SQLSTATEs come from the server's csv log: each session's application_name is '<tag>/<session>', and for every session the messages the tester printed must equal the messages the server logged, in order; a mismatch stops the run.
NULL prints as an empty cell in isolationtester output; an empty string prints the same way.

A session that continues after an error meets 'current transaction is aborted' (25P02) at its next write. Those follow-on errors stay in the row outputs, as after_abort in the index, and keep a history out of the GEN-anomaly-id pool.
The lock model that decides which interleavings cannot hang the tester is sound and incomplete; every lock wait the tester reported was one the model predicted.
The grid's 'half' split, the target counts and the retry patterns are design defaults [D], not measurements.
Nothing was emulated: no browser, phone, hosted service or other PostgreSQL version was involved. PGlite is a different instrument (W0-S08).

notes: Reference: PostgreSQL 18.6 (the postgres:18 image) on one node-postgres connection, in a fresh container started for this run and removed at its end. Compared: PGlite 0.5.11 under Node 22 and in a module worker in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit as shipped by Playwright 1.63.0, headless, in the Playwright container, served from a loopback server that sends no cross-origin isolation headers.
The browsers are desktop engines on a 20-CPU host, not phones; no timing in this record is a phone timing.

The access matrix is computed in plain code from S7's three read rules and compared with what each engine returns under SET ROLE. Equality between engines is exact on rows, row counts, SQLSTATE, message and detail; per-world results compare as SHA-256 hashes of the full visible-id maps, and the first three worlds keep their full maps in the result files.

The reference world is S7's W0 plus Risk (a team nested in Payments, with eli in it), ivy (a teamless user) and a revoked share of roadmap to gia. Generated worlds follow S7's ranges, with WF1 to WF3 true by construction, and each seed gives the same world in every engine (the world hash is compared).

The SQL under test is this harness's realization of S7.L4's policies and functions (the lesson's own text for the three read policies; the UPDATE and INSERT policies and user_teams are written here). The lab template's policies and harness do not exist yet.
The policy-subquery race under READ COMMITTED (catalog row H17) needs two sessions and cannot run on PGlite's single connection; it is not tested here.

PGlite's default connection role is the superuser postgres, which bypasses row security even on a forced table, so every RLS specimen switches role with SET ROLE first; the owner connection is emulated by SET ROLE to the table owner.
